title: Light as a form of energy
subject: physics
definition:
Light is a form of energy that enables us to see the objects around us. Without light, the world would be completely dark and we would not be able to see anything, no matter how large or colourful the objects are. Light carries energy from one place to another -- the most important example being sunlight, which travels across space from the Sun to the Earth and brings heat and light energy that supports all life on our planet. Because light can transfer energy from a source to a receiver, physicists classify it as a form of energy, just like heat energy, sound energy, and electrical energy.

A source of light is any object that gives out light. Sources of light are grouped into two kinds: natural sources and artificial (man-made) sources. Natural sources are those that exist in nature without human action. The most important natural source is the Sun, which is the chief source of light and heat for the Earth. Other natural sources include the stars, which are distant suns, and living things that produce their own light such as the firefly (jugnu), which glows at night, and certain glowing sea creatures. Fire, produced by burning wood or oil, is also a natural source of light.

Artificial sources are those made by human beings. Common examples include the electric bulb, the candle, the torch, and the LED (light-emitting diode). An electric bulb converts electrical energy into light energy; a candle burns wax to produce light; a torch uses a battery to power a small bulb or LED; and an LED is a modern, energy-efficient source that uses very little electricity and lasts a long time. Today LEDs are used in homes, streetlights, and even in Diwali decorations across Indian cities.

Objects around us can also be sorted into two groups based on light. Luminous objects are objects that give out their own light -- the Sun, a lit bulb, a burning candle, a firefly, and a star are all luminous. Non-luminous objects are objects that do not give out their own light but only become visible when light from a luminous source falls on them and is reflected into our eyes. A book, a chair, a tree, the Moon, and a human being are all non-luminous; we see them only because light bounces off them. The Moon is a special case -- it looks bright at night but it is non-luminous, because it only reflects sunlight.

A key property of light is that it travels in straight lines. This is called the rectilinear propagation of light. We can observe this when a beam of sunlight passes through a small hole in a dark room and forms a straight, narrow beam, or when the headlight of a car on a straight Indian highway at night shows a straight beam of light. Because light travels in straight lines, it cannot bend around corners on its own, and when something blocks it, a shadow is formed. This straight-line behaviour is the foundation for understanding shadows, eclipses, and reflection in later classes.
eli5: Light is a kind of energy that lets us see things. It comes from sources like the Sun (natural) and a bulb or torch (made by humans). Things that make their own light, like the Sun or a firefly, are luminous; things that only show up when light falls on them, like a book or the Moon, are non-luminous. Light always travels in straight lines, like water flowing through a straight pipe -- it never bends around corners on its own.

misconceptions.belief: The Moon is a luminous object because it shines brightly at night.
misconceptions.correction: The Moon is non-luminous. It does not produce its own light; it only reflects sunlight falling on it. A luminous object must give out its own light, like the Sun, a lit bulb, or a firefly. The CISCE examiner comments repeatedly warn that students give vague answers instead of citing the correct phenomenon -- here the correct reasoning is reflection of sunlight, not self-emission.

misconceptions.belief: Light can bend around corners, so we can see around a wall.
misconceptions.correction: Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation). It cannot bend around a corner on its own. That is why a wall blocks your view and why shadows have sharp edges. Bending of light happens only through special effects like reflection or refraction, which are taught in Classes 7 and 8 -- not by light itself turning a corner.

misconceptions.belief: A mirror is a luminous object because it shines.
misconceptions.correction: A mirror is non-luminous. It only reflects light from some other source. Confusing "shiny" or "bright-looking" with "luminous" is a common error; the test is whether the object itself produces light, not whether it looks bright.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State that light is a form of energy and name two natural and two artificial sources of light.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Light is a form of energy that enables us to see objects and carries energy from one place to another, for example from the Sun to the Earth. Natural sources of light are sources that exist in nature without human action. Two natural sources are the Sun and the firefly (jugnu); stars are also natural sources. Artificial sources are sources made by human beings. Two artificial sources are the electric bulb and the torch; a candle and an LED lamp are also artificial sources. The Sun is the most important natural source because it supplies almost all the light and heat we receive on Earth, while electric bulbs and LEDs are the most common artificial sources used in homes and schools. Being able to give one clear example of each type, with the correct label of natural or artificial, is what examiners expect.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why we are able to see a non-luminous object such as a book in a classroom, even though the book does not give out its own light.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A book is a non-luminous object, which means it does not produce its own light. We can still see it because light from a luminous source -- such as the Sun through a window or an electric bulb on the ceiling -- falls on the book. When this light strikes the surface of the book, some of it is reflected, or bounced back, in many directions. A small part of this reflected light enters our eyes, and that is what allows us to see the book. If the classroom were completely dark with no luminous source at all, no light would fall on the book, no light would be reflected into our eyes, and we would not be able to see the book even though it is still there. This shows that seeing a non-luminous object always depends on an external luminous source and on the reflection of light from that source into our eyes.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "The Moon is a luminous object because it glows brightly in the night sky, so it must be producing its own light just like the Sun." Evaluate this statement and explain whether it is correct or incorrect, with a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
The statement is incorrect. The Moon is a non-luminous object, not a luminous one, even though it appears bright in the night sky. The key distinction is between producing light and reflecting light. A luminous object is one that gives out its own light -- examples include the Sun, a lit electric bulb, a burning candle, a star, and a firefly. The Moon does not produce any light of its own; it has no internal source of light energy. Instead, sunlight falls on the Moon's surface and is reflected off it, and that reflected light travels to the Earth and enters our eyes. This is exactly the same way we see a non-luminous book in a classroom -- light from a luminous source (the Sun) falls on the object (the Moon) and is reflected into our eyes.

It is understandable why the student made this mistake: the Moon does look bright, especially on a clear night, and brightness can be confused with self-emission. However, brightness alone is not the test for luminous objects. The correct test is whether the object itself generates light. A fair evaluation must acknowledge that the student's observation (the Moon looks bright) is correct, but the conclusion (therefore it is luminous) is wrong. The Moon's brightness is borrowed brightness, not produced brightness. Evidence for this is that we only see the part of the Moon that is facing the Sun and is lit by it; the part not lit by the Sun is dark, which would not happen if the Moon produced its own light. This is also why the Moon shows phases -- the lit portion changes depending on the Sun's position. Therefore, the Moon is correctly classified as non-luminous, and the student's statement should be corrected.

diagnosticQuestions.question: In a dark room, you switch on a torch and point it at a chair. You then place a cardboard sheet between the torch and the chair. Describe what happens and explain it using the idea that light travels in straight lines.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: When the torch is switched on, light from the torch travels through the air in a straight beam toward the chair. Because light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation), the beam reaches the chair and lights it up, making the chair visible. When a cardboard sheet is placed between the torch and the chair, the cardboard blocks the straight path of the light. Since light cannot bend around the cardboard on its own, no light reaches the chair, and a shadow of the cardboard is formed on the side away from the torch. The chair now appears dark because no light is falling on it and therefore no light is being reflected from it into our eyes. This activity demonstrates two ideas together: light travels in straight lines, and when an opaque object blocks that straight path, a shadow is formed and objects behind the blocker cannot be lit by that source.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom activity to help Class 6 students discover that light travels in straight lines, using only objects commonly found at home or school. Describe the steps and what the students should observe.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A suitable activity is the "three-hole card" experiment. Take three stiff cardboard cards and make a small hole (about the size of a pea) in the centre of each. Stand the cards upright using stands or by folding the bottom edge, and place them in a row about 20 cm apart on a table, with all three holes at the same height. Ask a student to look through the holes while a candle or torch is placed on the other side, in line with the holes. When all three holes are in a straight line, the student can see the flame or light clearly. Now slide the middle card a little to one side so its hole is no longer in line. The student can no longer see the light, because the straight path is broken and light cannot bend around the cardboard. Students should observe that the light is visible only when the three holes form a straight line, and not visible when any one hole is out of line. This observation directly shows that light travels in straight lines -- the central idea of rectilinear propagation. The activity uses only cardboard, a candle or torch, and a ruler, all easily available, and it gives a clear, memorable result that students can explain in their own words.

masteryCriteria: Can state that light is a form of energy that enables us to see objects and carries energy from the Sun to the Earth; can name at least two natural sources (Sun, firefly, stars) and two artificial sources (electric bulb, candle, torch, LED) of light; can distinguish luminous objects (give out their own light -- Sun, lit bulb, firefly) from non-luminous objects (reflect light -- book, chair, Moon) and correctly classify the Moon as non-luminous; can state that light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation) and use this to explain why shadows form when light is blocked.

title: Reflection of light (plane mirror)
subject: physics
definition:
Reflection of light is the bouncing back of light rays when they strike a surface and cannot pass through it. When a beam of light travelling in a straight line hits a polished or shiny surface such as a plane mirror, it turns back into the same medium instead of entering the surface. This change of direction at the surface is called reflection, and it is the reason we are able to see objects that do not give out their own light -- the light from a source bounces off the object and reaches our eyes.

To describe reflection precisely, physicists use a set of key terms. The ray of light that falls on the reflecting surface is called the incident ray. The ray that bounces back into the same medium after striking the surface is called the reflected ray. The point where the incident ray meets the surface is called the point of incidence. The normal is an imaginary line drawn perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence -- it acts as the reference line from which all angles are measured. The angle between the incident ray and the normal is called the angle of incidence (written as i), and the angle between the reflected ray and the normal is called the angle of reflection (written as r). Both angles are always measured from the normal, never from the surface itself.

Reflection follows two laws. The first law states that the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection (i = r). The second law states that the incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal all lie in the same plane. Together these two laws govern every reflection, whether from a mirror, a sheet of water, or a wall.

A plane mirror is a flat, smooth, silvered reflecting surface that produces a clear, upright image of an object. Because its surface is perfectly smooth, all the parallel rays falling on it are reflected in the same direction -- this is called regular reflection, and it is why a plane mirror gives a sharp, well-defined image. In contrast, when light falls on a rough surface such as a sheet of paper, an unpolished wooden table, or a brick wall, the rays are scattered in many different directions because each tiny part of the surface faces a slightly different way. This is called diffuse reflection, and it is the reason rough surfaces do not form a clear image even though they still reflect light. A simple activity to demonstrate the laws is to direct a narrow beam of light from a ray box or a laser pointer at a plane mirror placed on a sheet of paper, mark the incident and reflected rays, draw the normal at the point of incidence, and measure the angles with a protractor -- the two angles will be found equal.
eli5: Imagine throwing a ball at a flat wall. It hits the wall and bounces back at the same angle it came in -- that is reflection, but with light instead of a ball. The line straight out from the wall is like a flagpole, and you measure the angles from that flagpole, not from the ground. A mirror is so smooth that light bounces back neatly and you see yourself; a rough wall scatters the light everywhere, so no clear picture forms.

misconceptions.belief: The angle of incidence and angle of reflection are measured from the mirror surface.
misconceptions.correction: Both angles are always measured from the normal -- the perpendicular line drawn at the point of incidence. Measuring from the surface gives the wrong values and the two angles will not appear equal even though the law i = r still holds. CISCE examiners have repeatedly observed that candidates incorrectly mark the angles of incidence and reflection in diagrams, losing marks.

misconceptions.belief: Diffuse reflection means the laws of reflection do not hold for rough surfaces.
misconceptions.correction: The two laws of reflection hold at every single point of a rough surface. Because each tiny part of a rough surface faces a different direction, the normal at each point is different, so parallel rays reflect in different directions. The rays still obey i = r at each point -- the scattering comes from the varying normals, not from a failure of the law.

misconceptions.belief: The normal is a real ray of light.
misconceptions.correction: The normal is an imaginary, dashed perpendicular line drawn only to measure angles. It is not light and it does not carry energy. Examiners have noted that candidates often fail to draw or label the normal correctly, or confuse it with a light ray, which leads to incorrect angle measurement.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define reflection of light and name the six key terms used to describe it, stating what each one means.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Reflection of light is the bouncing back of light rays into the same medium when they strike a surface they cannot pass through. The six key terms are: incident ray -- the ray of light falling on the surface; reflected ray -- the ray that bounces back into the same medium; point of incidence -- the point where the incident ray meets the reflecting surface; normal -- an imaginary line drawn perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence; angle of incidence (i) -- the angle between the incident ray and the normal; and angle of reflection (r) -- the angle between the reflected ray and the normal. Both angles are always measured from the normal, never from the surface itself. These six terms are the vocabulary needed to state and apply the two laws of reflection, and every diagram of reflection at a plane mirror must label each of them clearly with arrows on the rays and a dashed line for the normal.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 35 degrees to the mirror surface. Explain why the angle of incidence is 55 degrees, not 35 degrees, and state the angle of reflection.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The angle of incidence is defined as the angle between the incident ray and the normal, not between the incident ray and the mirror surface. The normal is perpendicular to the mirror, so it makes 90 degrees with the surface. If the incident ray makes 35 degrees with the surface, then it makes 90 minus 35, which is 55 degrees, with the normal. Therefore the angle of incidence i is 55 degrees. By the first law of reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, so the angle of reflection r is also 55 degrees. This question traps students who measure the angle from the surface instead of from the normal -- a mistake CISCE examiners have repeatedly flagged. Always identify the normal first, then measure both angles from it, to avoid this error.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student claims that a rough brick wall does not reflect light at all, which is why you cannot see your image in it. Evaluate this claim and explain what actually happens.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The claim is incorrect. A rough brick wall does reflect light -- in fact, it is the reason we can see the wall at all. If the wall did not reflect any light, it would appear completely black, like a shadow. What is different about a rough surface is the kind of reflection it produces. A plane mirror has a smooth, flat surface, so a set of parallel rays falling on it all meet normals that point in the same direction, and each ray reflects obeying i = r with the same geometry, sending all the rays back in one direction. This is regular reflection, and it forms a clear, sharp image. A brick wall, by contrast, is full of tiny bumps and hollows, each facing a slightly different way. At each tiny point the laws of reflection still hold -- i still equals r at that point -- but because the normal at each point points in a different direction, the parallel rays are scattered in many different directions. This is called diffuse reflection. The scattered rays do not carry the organised pattern needed to form an image, so you cannot see your reflection in the wall, even though the wall is reflecting plenty of light to your eyes. So the student has confused "no image" with "no reflection." The correct statement is: a rough surface reflects light by diffuse reflection, which scatters the rays and prevents image formation, but it does not stop reflecting light. The two laws of reflection hold at every point on the rough surface; it is the variation in the direction of the normal across the surface that causes the scattering.

diagnosticQuestions.question: In an activity, a student directs a ray of light at a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees. Draw a labelled diagram in words and state the angle the reflected ray makes with the mirror surface.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Draw the mirror as a horizontal straight line. At the point of incidence, draw the normal as a dashed vertical line perpendicular to the mirror, at 90 degrees to the surface. Draw the incident ray coming in from the upper left, making 40 degrees with the normal (and therefore 50 degrees with the mirror surface), with an arrow pointing towards the mirror. Draw the reflected ray going out to the upper right, making 40 degrees with the normal on the other side, with an arrow pointing away from the mirror. Label the angle between the incident ray and the normal as i = 40 degrees, and the angle between the reflected ray and the normal as r = 40 degrees, since by the first law of reflection i = r. The reflected ray makes 40 degrees with the normal, so it makes 90 minus 40, which is 50 degrees, with the mirror surface. The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane, satisfying the second law. This is the kind of labelled diagram CISCE examiners expect, with arrows on both rays and both angles clearly marked from the normal.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple experiment using a plane mirror, a ray box, a sheet of white paper, a pencil, and a protractor to verify the first law of reflection. Describe the steps and how you would use the results to confirm the law.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Place the sheet of white paper flat on a table and stand the plane mirror upright at one edge, supported so it does not move. Draw a straight line along the base of the mirror on the paper to mark the reflecting surface. Switch on the ray box and direct a narrow beam of light onto the mirror so that the incident ray, the reflected ray, and a clear point of incidence are all visible on the paper. Using the pencil, mark two dots on the incident beam and two dots on the reflected beam, and one dot at the point of incidence. Switch off the ray box and remove the mirror. Join the two dots on the incident side to draw the incident ray with an arrow pointing towards the mirror, and join the two dots on the other side to draw the reflected ray with an arrow pointing away. At the point of incidence, draw the normal as a dashed line perpendicular to the mirror line. Use the protractor to measure the angle between the incident ray and the normal -- this is the angle of incidence i. Then measure the angle between the reflected ray and the normal -- this is the angle of reflection r. Record both values. Repeat the activity with the ray box at three different angles, say 20 degrees, 40 degrees, and 60 degrees, recording i and r each time. If in every case the measured value of i equals the measured value of r within the limits of experimental error, the first law of reflection is confirmed. The results table should show i and r matching for each trial, demonstrating that the angle of incidence always equals the angle of reflection.

masteryCriteria: Can define reflection as the bouncing back of light from a surface and name the six key terms (incident ray, reflected ray, normal, point of incidence, angle of incidence i, angle of reflection r); can state the two laws of reflection (i = r; incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane); can identify and label the incident ray, reflected ray, normal, and the two angles on a diagram of a plane mirror; can distinguish regular reflection (smooth surface, clear image) from diffuse reflection (rough surface, no clear image) with one example each.

title: Image formation by plane mirror
subject: physics
definition:
A plane mirror is a flat, smooth reflecting surface that obeys the two laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane. When light from an object strikes a plane mirror, the mirror reflects the light into the observer's eye. The observer's brain traces the reflected rays straight back behind the mirror, where they appear to meet at a point. This apparent meeting point is the image of the object. Because the rays do not actually meet behind the mirror -- they only appear to do so -- the image is called a virtual image. A virtual image cannot be captured on a screen placed behind the mirror, unlike a real image which is formed by actual intersection of reflected or refracted rays and can be caught on a screen.

The image formed by a plane mirror has four well-defined properties that must be remembered together. First, it is virtual -- it cannot be projected on a screen. Second, it is erect (upright) -- it is not upside down. Third, it is the same size as the object -- neither magnified nor diminished. Fourth, it is laterally inverted -- the left side of the object appears as the right side of the image and vice versa. A fifth, equally important property concerns position: the image is formed at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. This means the object distance (distance of object from the mirror) equals the image distance (distance of image behind the mirror). The line joining the object and its image is perpendicular to the mirror surface.

Lateral inversion is the left-right reversal produced by a plane mirror. When you raise your right hand, your mirror image appears to raise its left hand. Text held up to a mirror appears reversed -- the word "AMBULANCE" is printed inverted on the front of an ambulance vehicle so that when a driver ahead looks in the rear-view mirror, the reversed letters appear correct and the driver can read the word AMBULANCE and give way. A simple ray diagram shows image formation by drawing at least two rays from a chosen point on the object to the mirror, applying the laws of reflection to draw the reflected rays, and then extending the reflected rays backwards (dashed lines) behind the mirror until they meet -- that meeting point is the image of that object point. Repeating for a second point gives the full image.
eli5: Stand in front of a flat mirror. You see a "twin" looking back at you -- the same size, standing upright, the same distance behind the glass as you are in front. But that twin is not really there; you cannot put a paper behind the mirror and catch the picture, so we call it a virtual image. The twin also swaps your left and right: when you wave your right hand, the twin waves its left. That swap is called lateral inversion.

misconceptions.belief: A plane mirror forms a real image.
misconceptions.correction: A real image is formed when reflected rays actually meet. In a plane mirror the reflected rays only appear to meet when extended backwards behind the mirror -- they never actually intersect there. So the image is virtual and cannot be caught on a screen. The CISCE 2024 examiner report (Question 13) notes candidates wrongly described the image as real and magnified; both claims are incorrect for a plane mirror.

misconceptions.belief: The image is smaller than the object because it looks smaller when I step back.
misconceptions.correction: The image is always the same size as the object. It only appears smaller because it is farther from your eye when you step back -- the same way a distant person looks smaller without actually shrinking. The actual image height equals the object height at all distances.

misconceptions.belief: The mirror flips the image upside down.
misconceptions.correction: A plane mirror does not invert top and bottom. The image is erect (upright). What reverses is front-to-back, which we perceive as a left-right swap -- lateral inversion. Top stays top, bottom stays bottom.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List the properties of the image formed by a plane mirror.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The image formed by a plane mirror has five key properties. First, it is virtual -- it cannot be captured on a screen placed behind the mirror because the reflected rays do not actually meet; they only appear to meet when extended backwards. Second, it is erect (upright) -- the top of the object remains the top of the image, so it is not upside down. Third, it is the same size as the object -- a 5 cm tall object produces a 5 cm tall image; there is no magnification or diminution. Fourth, it is laterally inverted -- the left side of the object appears as the right side of the image and vice versa, which is why your raised right hand appears as the image's raised left hand. Fifth, it is located at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of it -- if the object is 10 cm in front, the image is 10 cm behind. Together these five properties fully describe the image and should be stated together in any answer.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why the image formed by a plane mirror is called virtual and not real, using the idea of how the rays behave.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A real image is one formed by the actual intersection of reflected or refracted rays -- you can place a screen at that point and catch the picture. A virtual image, by contrast, is formed where rays only appear to meet when traced backwards; no actual crossing of rays takes place at the image location. When light from an object falls on a plane mirror, each ray reflects obeying the laws of reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection). The reflected rays travel out towards the observer's eye. The observer's brain, however, always assumes light travels in straight lines, so it extends each reflected ray backwards in a straight line behind the mirror. These backward extensions (drawn as dashed lines) meet at a point behind the mirror -- that point is the image. Because the real, solid reflected rays never actually pass through that point and never meet there, no screen placed behind the mirror will show any picture. Hence the image is virtual, not real. This is the fundamental difference between a plane mirror's image and the real image formed by, say, a pinhole camera where rays genuinely cross.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student writes, "A plane mirror forms a real, magnified, upside-down image behind the mirror." Evaluate this statement point by point and give the correct description.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is wrong on every count and reflects exactly the kind of confusion CISCE examiners flagged in the 2024 report (Question 13), where candidates "wrote that a real and magnified image is formed instead of a virtual image." Let us evaluate each claim. First, "real" is incorrect: the reflected rays from a plane mirror do not actually meet behind the mirror; they only appear to meet when extended backwards as dashed lines. Therefore no screen can catch the image, and the image is virtual, not real. Second, "magnified" is incorrect: the image formed by a plane mirror is always the same size as the object -- a 6 cm tall object gives a 6 cm tall image. There is no magnification or diminution at any object distance. The apparent change in size when you move towards or away from the mirror is a perspective effect due to changing distance from the eye, not a true change in image size. Third, "upside-down" is incorrect: the image is erect (upright). A plane mirror reverses front-to-back, which we perceive as a left-right swap (lateral inversion), but it does not interchange top and bottom. The top of the object remains the top of the image. The only correct part of the student's statement is that the image is located behind the mirror. The correct description is: "The image formed by a plane mirror is virtual, erect, the same size as the object, laterally inverted, and situated at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of it." A student who memorises this exact chain of five properties will avoid all three errors in the statement.

diagnosticQuestions.question: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a plane mirror. (a) How far behind the mirror is the image? (b) How far is the image from the object? (c) If the object is 8 cm tall, how tall is the image? Draw a labelled ray diagram in words.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: (a) The image is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, so the image is 15 cm behind the mirror. (b) The object is 15 cm in front and the image is 15 cm behind, so the total distance between object and image is 15 cm + 15 cm = 30 cm. (c) The image is the same size as the object, so an 8 cm tall object produces an 8 cm tall image. For the ray diagram in words: draw the mirror as a vertical line with hatching on the back (right) side; draw the object as an upright arrow 8 cm tall, 15 cm to the left of the mirror, with its base on a horizontal reference line perpendicular to the mirror. From the tip of the arrow draw two incident rays to the mirror -- one straight (perpendicular) to the mirror and one at an angle. Draw the normal (dotted) at each point of incidence. The perpendicular ray reflects straight back along its own path; the angled ray reflects with angle of reflection equal to angle of incidence. Extend both reflected rays backwards behind the mirror as dashed lines; they meet 15 cm behind the mirror at a point 8 cm above the reference line. Join this point to the point on the reference line 15 cm behind the mirror to draw the image arrow. Label O (object), I (image), object distance = 15 cm, image distance = 15 cm, and put arrows on every ray.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple home activity that demonstrates two properties of a plane mirror image -- same distance behind the mirror and lateral inversion. Describe what you would use, what you would do, and what you would observe.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To demonstrate the same-distance property, take a plain plane mirror, a small upright object such as a pencil standing on its base, and a ruler. Place the mirror vertically against a wall. Stand the pencil 10 cm in front of the mirror, measured with the ruler. Now look from the side and estimate where the image of the pencil appears to be behind the mirror; you will find it looks 10 cm behind the glass. To confirm, place a second identical pencil behind the mirror and slide it until, looking from the front, it seems to coincide exactly with the image of the front pencil -- you will find the back pencil is also 10 cm behind the mirror. This shows image distance equals object distance. To demonstrate lateral inversion, write the word "AMBULANCE" in bold capital letters on a strip of paper. Hold the strip facing the mirror and read the reflection: the letters appear reversed left-to-right, so "A" looks like a mirror-A and the whole word reads backwards. Now write "AMBULANCE" already reversed on another strip; hold it up and the reflection reads correctly as "AMBULANCE" -- exactly why ambulances paint the word inverted on their front. These two quick activities make the same-distance and lateral-inversion properties visible without any special equipment, and they turn the abstract properties into something the student can see and verify.

masteryCriteria: Can state the five properties of a plane mirror image in one chain -- virtual, erect, same size as the object, laterally inverted, and at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front (e.g., object 10 cm in front gives image 10 cm behind). Can explain lateral inversion with a concrete example such as the right hand appearing as the left hand, or the word AMBULANCE printed inverted so it reads correctly in a rear-view mirror. Can draw a simple ray diagram with two rays from an object point, normals at the points of incidence, reflected rays obeying angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, dashed backward extensions meeting at the image, and labels for object, image, object distance and image distance. Can distinguish a virtual image (cannot be caught on a screen) from a real image (can be caught on a screen).

title: Concave mirror and its properties
subject: physics
definition: A concave mirror, also called a converging mirror, is a spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is curved inwards, like the inside of a shiny spoon. In a concave mirror the reflecting surface faces the centre of the hollow sphere of which the mirror is a part, so parallel rays of light falling on it are bent inward and meet (converge) at a single point in front of the mirror called the principal focus (F). To describe a concave mirror precisely, several key terms are used. The pole (P) is the centre of the reflecting surface -- the geometric midpoint of the mirror. The centre of curvature (C) is the centre of the hollow glass sphere of which the mirror forms a part; it always lies in front of a concave mirror, on the same side as the reflecting surface. The radius of curvature (R) is the distance between the pole (P) and the centre of curvature (C), that is, the radius of that imaginary sphere. The principal axis is the straight line passing through the pole (P) and the centre of curvature (C); it is the mirror's axis of symmetry. The principal focus (F) is the point on the principal axis where rays of light travelling parallel to the principal axis, after reflection from the mirror, actually meet. Because the reflected rays really pass through F, the focus of a concave mirror is real. The focal length (f) is the distance from the pole (P) to the principal focus (F); for a spherical mirror of small aperture, f is approximately equal to half the radius of curvature (f = R/2). The chief property of a concave mirror is that it converges a parallel beam of light to a real focus in front of the mirror, which is why it is called a converging mirror. This distinguishes it from a plane mirror, whose reflecting surface is flat and which neither converges nor diverges parallel rays -- it simply reflects them according to the law of reflection, forming a virtual, erect, same-size image behind the mirror. The inward-curved surface of a concave mirror, by contrast, makes each reflected ray obey the same law of reflection but tilt inward, so the rays meet at F. A ray diagram for a concave mirror shows several rays parallel to the principal axis striking the curved surface and, after reflection, all passing through the principal focus F. Common examples include the inside of a polished spoon, a dentist's small mouth mirror (which gives a magnified view of the teeth), a shaving mirror, the reflector behind a torch bulb or a car headlight, and the large parabolic dish of a solar furnace at places like Mount Abu in Rajasthan that concentrates sunlight to heat water.
eli5: Think of the inside of a shiny spoon. That inward-bowl surface is a concave mirror. The middle of the bowl is the pole. The big invisible ball the bowl came from has a centre -- that is the centre of curvature. Rays coming in straight and parallel, like sunlight, bounce off the curved bowl and all meet at one spot called the focus. That is why it is a "converging" mirror -- it gathers light to a point, unlike a flat mirror that just sends it back straight.

misconceptions.belief: The centre of curvature of a concave mirror lies behind the mirror, like the image in a plane mirror.
misconceptions.correction: For a concave mirror the reflecting surface faces the inside of the imaginary sphere, so the centre of curvature C lies in front of the mirror, on the same side as the reflecting surface. Only for a convex mirror does C lie behind. This matters because examiners (CISCE PPA 2019, 2024) repeatedly report students using the wrong sign for radius of curvature R -- confusion that begins with not knowing where C is.

misconceptions.belief: A concave mirror always forms a real image, so its focus is virtual.
misconceptions.correction: The principal focus of a concave mirror is real because reflected rays actually pass through F; that is exactly why parallel rays converge there. Whether the image of an object is real or virtual depends on where the object is placed -- close to the mirror (between P and F) the image is virtual and magnified, farther away it is real and inverted. At Class 7 we only need to know that the focus itself is real; image cases come later.

misconceptions.belief: A concave mirror and a plane mirror reflect light differently -- one follows the law of reflection, the other does not.
misconceptions.correction: Both mirrors obey the same two laws of reflection at every point. The difference is the shape of the reflecting surface: a plane mirror is flat so parallel rays stay parallel after reflection, whereas a concave mirror is inward-curved so the normals tilt and the reflected rays converge to F. The law of reflection is the same; the geometry of the surface is what differs.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a concave mirror and name its key parts with their symbols.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A concave mirror (also called a converging mirror) is a spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is curved inwards, like the inside of a polished spoon. Its key parts are: the pole (P), the centre point of the reflecting surface; the centre of curvature (C), the centre of the hollow glass sphere of which the mirror is a part, lying in front of the mirror; the radius of curvature (R), the distance from P to C; the principal axis, the straight line passing through P and C; the principal focus (F), the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet after reflection; and the focal length (f), the distance from P to F. Because the reflected rays actually pass through F, the focus of a concave mirror is real, and for a small-aperture mirror f is approximately R/2.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why a concave mirror is called a converging mirror, using the law of reflection.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A concave mirror is called a converging mirror because a beam of rays travelling parallel to its principal axis, after reflection, meets (converges) at a single point in front of the mirror called the principal focus F. At every point on the curved surface the two laws of reflection hold -- the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane. Because the surface curves inwards, the normal at each point is tilted towards the principal axis. A ray striking above the axis has its normal pointing slightly downward, so the reflected ray is bent down towards the axis; a ray striking below the axis is bent upward. The on-axis ray reflects back along the axis. All these reflected rays therefore cross the principal axis at the same point F. Thus the inward curvature, combined with the ordinary law of reflection, is what makes the mirror converge parallel rays -- which is why it is named a converging mirror.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student states, "A concave mirror and a plane mirror are both mirrors, so they behave in exactly the same way -- both form virtual, erect, same-size images." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is incorrect and oversimplified. While it is true that both a concave mirror and a plane mirror obey the same two laws of reflection at every point on their surfaces, their behaviour is very different because the shape of the reflecting surface is different. A plane mirror has a flat reflecting surface, so the normals at all points are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the mirror. Parallel rays falling on it remain parallel after reflection, and the image of any object is always virtual, erect, laterally inverted, the same size as the object, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. A concave mirror, by contrast, has an inward-curved reflecting surface, so the normals at different points point in slightly different directions, all tilting towards the principal axis. Parallel rays falling on a concave mirror are therefore reflected so that they converge at a real principal focus F in front of the mirror. The image formed by a concave mirror depends on the position of the object: when the object is placed very close to the mirror (between P and F) the image is virtual, erect and magnified -- which is why a dentist's mirror or a shaving mirror is concave; when the object is placed farther away, beyond C, the image becomes real, inverted and diminished. So the two mirrors share the same law of reflection but produce very different images because of their different geometries. The student is right that both are mirrors obeying the same law, but wrong to conclude that they behave identically; the curvature is the decisive factor. At Class 7 level we focus on the converging property and the fact that the focus is real, leaving the full set of image cases to later classes.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Draw a ray diagram for a concave mirror showing two parallel rays incident on it and label P, C, F, principal axis and radius of curvature. Describe what happens to the rays after reflection.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Draw a concave mirror as a vertical arc opening to the left, with its reflecting (inner) surface facing left. Mark the midpoint of the arc as the pole P. Draw a horizontal straight line through P -- this is the principal axis. On this axis, to the left of the mirror (in front, on the reflecting side), mark the centre of curvature C at a distance R from P. Halfway between P and C, mark the principal focus F, so that PF = f and PC = R, with f = R/2 for a small-aperture mirror. Now draw two rays coming from the left, parallel to the principal axis, one just above the axis and one just below, both striking the curved surface. At each point of incidence draw the normal pointing towards C (since the normal to a spherical surface passes through its centre). Applying the law of reflection, the upper ray reflects downward and the lower ray reflects upward; both reflected rays cross the principal axis at F. The ray travelling exactly along the axis reflects back along itself and also passes through F. Thus all parallel rays converge at the real focus F in front of the mirror, demonstrating the converging property of a concave mirror.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple device that uses a concave mirror to collect sunlight for heating water, and explain which property of the concave mirror makes your design work.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would design a small solar water heater using a shallow concave (converging) mirror dish, about 50 cm across, mounted on a stand that can be tilted to face the Sun. At the principal focus F of the dish -- found by pointing the dish at the Sun and locating the bright spot where the reflected light is sharpest -- I would fix a blackened copper cup filled with water, insulated on the outside to reduce heat loss. The key property used is convergence: a concave mirror reflects a large beam of parallel sunlight falling on its inward-curved surface and brings all the reflected rays together at the single real focus F in front of the mirror. Because all the energy spread over the whole dish area is concentrated into the small cup at F, the water in the cup heats up rapidly -- far faster than it would if simply left in the open Sun. This is exactly how large solar dish concentrators work, for example the solar furnace installations near Mount Abu in Rajasthan, which use big concave (parabolic) reflectors to focus sunlight and generate high temperatures for cooking and industrial heating. The design shows that the converging property of a concave mirror is not just a diagram on paper but a practical tool for collecting and concentrating energy.

masteryCriteria: Can define a concave mirror as a spherical mirror with an inward-curved reflecting surface that converges parallel rays to a real focus F. Can identify and label the pole (P), centre of curvature (C), radius of curvature (R), principal axis, principal focus (F) and focal length (f), stating that C and F lie in front of the mirror and that f = R/2 for a small-aperture mirror. Can explain, using the law of reflection, why parallel rays converge at F (inward curve tilts the normals so reflected rays bend towards the axis). Can distinguish a concave mirror from a plane mirror (curved vs flat reflecting surface; converging vs non-converging; real focus vs no focus) and give at least three real uses (dentist's mirror, shaving mirror, torch/headlight reflector, solar furnace).

title: Convex mirror and its properties
subject: physics
definition:
A convex mirror, also called a diverging mirror, is a spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is curved outwards -- that is, the bulging, polished side of the spherical glass faces the light. The simplest way to picture it is to imagine the back of a shiny steel spoon: the outward-curved surface that you see is exactly the kind of surface a convex mirror uses. Because the surface bulges towards the incoming light, rays falling on it are reflected in such a way that they spread apart, or diverge. This is the defining property of a convex mirror and is the reason it is also known as a diverging mirror.

Like every spherical mirror, a convex mirror has a set of key terms that must be understood. The pole (P) is the geometric centre of the reflecting surface -- the single point at the middle of the outward bulge. The centre of curvature (C) is the centre of the imaginary sphere of which the mirror forms a part; for a convex mirror, C lies behind the mirror because the reflecting surface bulges away from the centre of that sphere. The principal axis is the straight line passing through the pole (P) and the centre of curvature (C). The principal focus (F) is the point on the principal axis through which all rays parallel to the principal axis appear to pass after reflection -- and here is the crucial difference from a concave mirror: in a convex mirror the reflected rays do not actually meet, they only appear to come from a point behind the mirror, so F is a virtual focus located behind the reflecting surface. The focal length (f) is the distance between the pole (P) and the principal focus (F); for a convex mirror f is taken as positive in the standard convention, but at Class 7 level we only need to know that f is the distance PF and that F lies behind the mirror.

The most important property of a convex mirror is that it always diverges a beam of parallel rays so that they appear to come from a single point (the focus) behind the mirror. Because the rays spread out, a convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished (smaller than the object) image, no matter where the object is placed in front of it. As a result of this spreading, a convex mirror captures a much wider field of view than a plane mirror or a concave mirror of the same size -- it shows more of the surroundings in a single glance, though everything looks smaller.

These properties make convex mirrors extremely useful in everyday life. The most common example is the rear-view and side mirror of a car, scooter or bus: the outward-curved glass gives the driver a wider view of the road behind, including traffic in adjacent lanes, even though the vehicles appear smaller and slightly farther away than they really are. This is why such mirrors carry the printed warning "objects in the mirror are closer than they appear". A second everyday use is the large security mirror fitted high in a corner of a shop, supermarket or ATM lobby so that staff can watch many aisles at once and spot shoplifters. Convex mirrors are also used at blind corners and sharp bends on hilly roads (for example on the winding roads of the Himalayan foothills) so that drivers coming from opposite directions can see each other before reaching the corner.
eli5: Imagine the back of a shiny steel spoon -- that outward bulge is a convex mirror. Because the surface curves out, when light bounces off it the rays spread apart instead of crossing. So everything you see in it looks smaller but you can see a lot more at once. That is why car side mirrors and shop security mirrors use this shape: you trade size for a wider view, and the image always stays upright.

misconceptions.belief: The focus of a convex mirror is in front of the mirror, where the reflected rays meet.
misconceptions.correction: The reflected rays from a convex mirror never actually meet -- they diverge. They only appear to come from a point behind the mirror, so the principal focus (F) is virtual and lies behind the reflecting surface, not in front. CISCE examiners (PPA 2019) noted that many candidates mishandle sign and position for curved mirrors; remembering that F is behind the mirror for a convex mirror prevents this error.

misconceptions.belief: A convex mirror is used in car headlights and shaving mirrors.
misconceptions.correction: Those are uses of a concave mirror, which converges light. A convex mirror is used where a wide view is needed -- rear-view and side mirrors of vehicles, security mirrors in shops, and mirrors at blind road corners. CISCE examiners (PPA 2019, Q7) specifically observed that students mix up the uses of concave and convex mirrors and recommended that teachers familiarise students with the correct applications of each.

misconceptions.belief: A convex mirror can form a real, inverted image if the object is far enough away.
misconceptions.correction: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image, no matter where the object is placed in front of it. Because the reflected rays always diverge, they can never actually meet in front of the mirror, so a real image is impossible.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a convex mirror and name its key parts.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A convex mirror (also called a diverging mirror) is a spherical mirror whose reflecting surface is curved outwards -- the bulging, polished side of a spherical glass faces the incoming light. Its key parts are: the pole (P), which is the centre point of the reflecting surface; the centre of curvature (C), which is the centre of the imaginary sphere of which the mirror is a part and which lies behind the mirror; the principal axis, the straight line passing through P and C; the principal focus (F), the point on the principal axis through which rays parallel to the axis appear to pass after reflection -- a virtual point behind the mirror; and the focal length (f), the distance from the pole P to the focus F. Because the surface bulges outwards, a beam of parallel rays falling on it is reflected so that the rays spread apart, or diverge, and seem to come from F behind the mirror.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why does a convex mirror diverge a beam of parallel rays, and why does this make its focus virtual and located behind the mirror?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Each ray that strikes a convex mirror obeys the ordinary law of reflection -- the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal at the point of incidence. However, because the reflecting surface curves outwards, the normal at each point points in a slightly different direction, tilting away from the principal axis as we move from the pole towards the edges. When a set of parallel rays strikes this curved surface, each ray is reflected at a slightly different angle such that the reflected rays fan outwards -- they diverge instead of remaining parallel or converging. Since the reflected rays move away from one another in front of the mirror, they never actually meet in front of it. If we extend these diverging rays backwards, behind the mirror, the extensions appear to meet at a single point on the principal axis. That point is the principal focus (F), and because only the backward extensions meet there while the real rays do not, F is a virtual focus lying behind the mirror. This is the opposite of a concave mirror, where the reflected rays actually meet in front and the focus is real.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student states: "A plane mirror gives a wider field of view than a convex mirror because it does not shrink the image, so it should be preferred for a car's rear-view mirror." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is incorrect on two counts. First, the claim about field of view is wrong. A convex mirror actually provides a wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size, because its outward-curving surface gathers light from a larger portion of the surroundings and bends the reflected rays outward, packing more of the scene into the small image. A plane mirror, being flat, reflects each ray at the same angle and shows only a narrow strip of what is behind the viewer; to see more, the mirror would have to be made much larger, which is impractical on a vehicle. Second, the student's reasoning that "no shrinking means a better mirror" confuses image size with usefulness. For a rear-view mirror, the driver's priority is not to see the vehicle behind at its true size but to be aware of as much of the road as possible -- vehicles in adjacent lanes, two-wheelers approaching from the sides, and pedestrians near the rear corners. The convex mirror achieves exactly this by accepting a diminished (smaller) image in exchange for a much wider field of view. The image is always virtual, erect and diminished, which is perfectly acceptable for the purpose of awareness. This is why every car, bus and truck uses convex glass for its side mirrors and prints the warning "objects in the mirror are closer than they appear" -- the trade-off of size for view is deliberate and beneficial. A plane mirror would leave dangerous blind spots on either side. Therefore the convex mirror, not the plane mirror, is the correct and safer choice for a rear-view application.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You are asked to install a mirror at a sharp blind hairpin bend on a hilly road near Mussoorie so that two vehicles approaching from opposite directions can see each other. Which type of mirror would you choose and why? Describe what each driver will see.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would choose a convex mirror and mount it on the inner side of the bend, facing both approaching directions. A convex mirror is the correct choice because its outward-curved reflecting surface diverges the reflected rays and produces a wide field of view, allowing each driver to see traffic coming from the opposite direction well before reaching the corner. A plane mirror would show only a narrow strip of the road and would have to be very large to be useful, while a concave mirror would converge the rays and give a narrow, distorted view. With the convex mirror in place, each driver will see a virtual, erect and diminished image of the approaching vehicle -- the image will be smaller than the actual vehicle, but it will be clearly visible from a distance and will cover a broad stretch of the road around the bend. Because the image is upright and shows a wide area, the driver can judge the direction from which the other vehicle is coming and slow down or stop in time. This is exactly why the Public Works Department installs convex mirrors at blind corners on mountain roads throughout the Himalayan foothills.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a small roadside shop in a busy market. You want the shopkeeper to be able to watch the whole shop floor while sitting at the cash counter, and you also want passing customers to see what is inside the shop from the street. Propose where and how you would use convex mirrors, and explain the physics behind each placement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would install two convex mirrors. The first, a large one, would be mounted high in the corner of the shop opposite the cash counter, angled downwards so that it faces the rows of shelves and the entrance. Because a convex mirror diverges light and gives a wide field of view, this single mirror will let the shopkeeper see almost every aisle at once as a virtual, erect and diminished image. Even though the customers and goods appear smaller, the shopkeeper can detect any unusual movement or shoplifting attempt across the whole floor -- something a plane mirror of the same size could never achieve. The second, a smaller convex mirror, would be placed just outside the entrance, angled towards the interior, so that a customer walking past on the street can glance at it and see a broad view of the goods inside without stepping in. Again the physics is the same: the outward-curved surface spreads the reflected rays, gathering light from a large interior area and presenting it as a compact, upright image. In both placements the key properties being exploited are the wide field of view and the always-virtual, always-erect, always-diminished image that a convex mirror produces regardless of object position. This design uses one mirror for security and one for advertisement, both relying on the same diverging behaviour of the convex surface.

masteryCriteria: Can define a convex mirror as a spherical mirror with its reflecting surface curved outwards (diverging mirror) and can identify the pole (P), centre of curvature (C, behind the mirror), principal axis, principal focus (F, virtual, behind the mirror) and focal length (f = PF); can explain that a convex mirror diverges parallel rays so they appear to come from a virtual focus behind the mirror and always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image; can state at least two everyday uses (rear-view/side mirrors of vehicles, security mirrors in shops, mirrors at blind road corners) with the correct reason (wide field of view).

title: Image formation by concave mirror
subject: physics
definition:
Image formation by a concave mirror describes how a converging mirror produces an image of an object placed in front of it, and how the nature, position and size of that image change as the object is moved to different positions along the principal axis. A concave mirror is a converging mirror whose reflecting surface curves inward; it has a pole (P), a centre of curvature (C) at twice the focal length, a principal focus (F) at the midpoint of P and C, and a principal axis joining P, F and C. To locate the image of any object we use a ray diagram in which two standard rays are drawn from the top of the object and their reflected rays are traced using the laws of reflection. The two standard rays used at Class 7 level are: (i) a ray travelling parallel to the principal axis, which after reflection passes through the principal focus F; and (ii) a ray passing through the centre of curvature C, which strikes the mirror normally and reflects back along its own path. The point where the two reflected rays (or their backward extensions) meet gives the position of the top of the image; dropping this point to the principal axis gives the full image.

Five object positions must be mastered. (1) Object between pole P and focus F: the two reflected rays diverge, so they are extended backwards behind the mirror; they appear to meet and form a virtual, erect and magnified image behind the mirror -- this is the makeup-mirror or shaving-mirror case. (2) Object at focus F: the reflected rays become parallel to each other and to the principal axis, so they meet only at infinity; the image is real, inverted and highly magnified, formed at infinity -- the searchlight/reflecting-lamp case. (3) Object between focus F and centre of curvature C: the reflected rays meet in front of the mirror at a point beyond C; the image is real, inverted and magnified -- used in film projectors and in some astronomical setups. (4) Object at centre of curvature C: the image forms at C itself; it is real, inverted and the same size as the object. (5) Object beyond centre of curvature C: the reflected rays meet between F and C; the image is real, inverted and diminished -- this is the case used by a dentist's concave mirror or a solar furnace concentrator, where a small bright image is wanted.

The key pattern to remember is that as the object moves away from the mirror (from P towards infinity), the real image moves from infinity towards F, becomes smaller, and the virtual case occurs only when the object is within the focal length. Real images are always inverted and can be caught on a screen; virtual images are always erect and cannot be caught on a screen. No mirror formula (1/v + 1/u = 1/f) or magnification formula (m = -v/u or m = hi/ho) is used at this stage; all conclusions are drawn from the ray diagrams themselves.
eli5: A concave mirror is like a shiny spoon that curves inward. Where you stand in front of it decides what you see. Stand very close (within the focus) and you see a big, upright, fake-you behind the spoon -- that's a virtual, magnified image, like a makeup mirror. Stand far away (beyond the centre of curvature) and the spoon throws a small, upside-down, real-you onto a screen in front of it. Move around and the picture changes -- close gives big and upright, far gives small and upside-down.

misconceptions.belief: Students think a virtual image can be caught on a screen.
misconceptions.correction: A real image is formed where reflected rays actually meet in front of the mirror, so it can be caught on a screen. A virtual image is formed where the rays only appear to meet behind the mirror, so it cannot be caught on a screen -- you see it by looking into the mirror. The between-P-and-F case is the only virtual case for a concave mirror.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Name the five standard object positions in front of a concave mirror and for each state whether the image is real or virtual, erect or inverted, and magnified, diminished or same size.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The five positions and their images are: (1) Object between pole P and focus F -- image is virtual, erect and magnified, formed behind the mirror. (2) Object at focus F -- image is real, inverted and highly magnified, formed at infinity. (3) Object between focus F and centre of curvature C -- image is real, inverted and magnified, formed beyond C. (4) Object at centre of curvature C -- image is real, inverted and the same size as the object, formed at C itself. (5) Object beyond centre of curvature C -- image is real, inverted and diminished, formed between F and C. The pattern is that only the closest position (within the focal length) gives a virtual image; all other positions give real, inverted images, and as the object moves away from the mirror the real image moves from infinity towards F and becomes smaller.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why a concave mirror used as a shaving mirror must have the face placed between the pole and the focus, and not at or beyond the focus.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A shaving mirror is meant to show an enlarged, upright image of the face so that small details can be seen clearly. For a concave mirror, an erect and magnified image is obtained only when the object is placed between the pole P and the principal focus F. In this position the two standard rays -- one parallel to the axis reflecting through F, and one through C reflecting back along its path -- diverge after reflection; their backward extensions meet behind the mirror to form a virtual, erect and magnified image. Because the image is virtual it cannot be caught on a screen, but it can be seen by looking into the mirror, which is exactly how a shaving mirror is used. If the face were placed at F, the reflected rays would become parallel and the image would form at infinity, which is useless for viewing. If the face were placed at or beyond C, the image would be real, inverted and diminished or same-size -- an upside-down picture behind the mirror is of no use for shaving. Hence the between-P-and-F position is the only one that gives the required upright, enlarged, viewable image.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student states: "A concave mirror always forms a real image because it is a converging mirror, so the image is always inverted and can always be caught on a screen." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is incorrect and reflects a common over-generalisation. While it is true that a concave mirror is a converging mirror and that it forms real, inverted images for most object positions, the word "always" makes the statement wrong. A concave mirror forms a real, inverted image only when the object is placed at or beyond the principal focus F -- that is, at F, between F and C, at C, or beyond C. In all these cases the reflected rays actually meet in front of the mirror, so the image is real, inverted and can be caught on a screen. However, when the object is placed between the pole P and the focus F, the reflected rays diverge after reflection and do not meet in front of the mirror at all; they only appear to meet when extended backwards behind the mirror. This produces a virtual, erect and magnified image that cannot be caught on a screen. The CISCE examiner reports for 2024 and 2025 (Question 13) explicitly note that many candidates lost marks by writing "real and magnified" when the correct answer for an object between P and F is "virtual and magnified" -- exactly the error this statement encourages. Therefore the correct position-dependent rule is: real and inverted for objects at or beyond F; virtual and erect for objects between P and F. The converging nature of the mirror does not guarantee a real image in every case; the object position relative to the focus is the deciding factor. A balanced view is that the converging property explains why most positions give real images, but the special within-focus case is the exception that must be remembered.

diagnosticQuestions.question: An object is placed beyond the centre of curvature of a concave mirror. Draw the ray diagram in words and state the nature, position and size of the image. Where is this case used in everyday life?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Draw the concave mirror with pole P, principal axis, focus F and centre of curvature C marked, with C at twice the focal length from P. Place an upright arrow (the object) on the axis beyond C, farther from the mirror than C is. From the tip of the arrow draw ray 1 parallel to the principal axis; after reflection it passes through F. Draw ray 2 from the tip straight through C; it strikes the mirror normally and reflects back along its own path through C. The two reflected rays meet at a point between F and C, in front of the mirror. Drop this point to the axis to get the image. The image is real (rays actually meet), inverted (the image arrow points down), and diminished (smaller than the object), and it is located between F and C. A practical use is a solar furnace concentrator or a dentist's head mirror used at a distance, where a small, bright, real image of a distant source is wanted on a small area. Another use is in some torch reflectors where a small bright image of the bulb is needed.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple tabletop demonstration using a concave mirror and a small lit candle that allows a student to see all five image cases one after another, and describe what the student should observe in each case.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Take a concave mirror mounted vertically on a stand, a small lit candle as the object, and a small white screen (a piece of cardboard) that can be moved along the principal axis. First measure the focal length f by focusing a distant window image on the screen; mark F on the axis and mark C at 2f. Case 1: Place the candle between P and F. Move the screen everywhere in front -- no image is caught. Look into the mirror: a large, upright, virtual image of the flame is seen behind the mirror. Case 2: Place the candle at F. The reflected rays come out nearly parallel; no image is caught on the screen at any finite distance, and looking into the mirror shows a very wide, blurred field -- the image is at infinity. Case 3: Place the candle between F and C. Move the screen beyond C until a sharp, large, upside-down image of the flame appears -- real, inverted, magnified. Case 4: Place the candle at C. The sharp image forms at C itself, upside down and the same size as the flame. Case 5: Move the candle beyond C. The sharp image now appears between F and C, upside down and smaller than the flame. By recording the image position, nature and size for each case, the student directly verifies the five ray-diagram predictions. The demonstration also shows that only Case 1 gives a virtual image and that the real image moves towards F and shrinks as the candle is moved away from the mirror.

masteryCriteria: Can draw the ray diagram for at least three of the five object positions using the two standard rays (parallel-to-axis through F, and through C reflecting back); can state for each of the five positions whether the image is real or virtual, erect or inverted, and magnified, diminished or same size; can explain that only an object between P and F gives a virtual image and that all other positions give real, inverted images; can identify a practical use for each case (shaving mirror, searchlight, projector, same-size reference, solar furnace).

title: Image formation by convex mirror
subject: physics
definition:
A convex mirror is a spherical mirror that bulges outward towards the light source, and its reflecting surface curves away from the incident rays. Because the surface curves outward, any ray of light striking it is reflected outward -- the mirror diverges the reflected rays. This single physical fact -- that reflected rays always spread apart -- is what determines every property of the image a convex mirror forms. When an object is placed in front of a convex mirror, the image is formed at the point where the reflected rays (or their backward extensions) appear to meet. Since the reflected rays actually diverge after reflection, they never meet in front of the mirror in real space. They only appear to meet when extended backwards behind the mirror. Therefore the image is always virtual -- it cannot be caught on a screen. Because the backward extensions meet behind the mirror at a smaller distance than the object is in front, the image is always diminished (smaller than the object). And because the image is formed by rays that appear to come from behind the mirror, the top of the image points the same way as the top of the object, so the image is always erect (upright). These three properties -- virtual, erect, and diminished -- hold for every position of the object, whether the object is very close to the mirror, very far away, or anywhere in between. This is unlike a concave mirror, where the image changes nature with object position.

To construct the image by a ray diagram, two standard rays are drawn from the top of the object. Ray 1 travels parallel to the principal axis; after striking the convex mirror it reflects outward along a direction that, when extended backwards behind the mirror, passes through the principal focus (F). Ray 2 travels towards the centre of curvature (C) of the mirror; because it strikes the mirror along the normal (the line joining the point of incidence to C), it is reflected back along its own path. The point where the two reflected rays (extended backwards behind the mirror) appear to intersect is the top of the image. Dropping a perpendicular from this point to the principal axis gives the base of the image. The image always lies between the principal focus (F) and the pole (P) of the mirror, behind the reflecting surface.

Because a convex mirror always gives a small, upright view of a large region, it is used wherever a wide field of view is needed. The rear-view mirror of a car (the side mirrors are often convex, marked "objects in mirror are closer than they appear") gives the driver a compressed but complete view of the road behind. Security mirrors in shops, at blind corners, and in parking lots give a single glance view of a wide area. The diminished image is a trade-off the user accepts in exchange for seeing more at once.
eli5: A convex mirror is like a spoon's back that bulges out. It bends light outward, so the light rays spread apart after bouncing off. Because they spread apart, they never really meet in front -- they only seem to meet behind the mirror. So you always see a small, upright, fake picture that you cannot catch on a screen. That is why car side mirrors and shop security mirrors use it: you see more of the scene, just smaller.

misconceptions.belief: A convex mirror can form a real image if the object is placed far away." This is the exact error CISCE examiners flagged in PPA 2024 and 2025 (Question 13): candidates wrote that a real and magnified image is formed.
misconceptions.correction: A convex mirror always diverges the reflected rays, so they never actually meet in front of the mirror -- they only meet when extended backwards behind the mirror. A real image requires actual rays to converge in front; since that never happens here, the image is always virtual, regardless of object position.

misconceptions.belief: The image position depends on whether the object is at F, between C and F, or behind F, like in a concave mirror." Examiners noted candidates wrongly mention these positions.
misconceptions.correction: Those six cases belong to the concave mirror lesson. For a convex mirror there is only one case: object anywhere in front, image always between F and P behind the mirror, virtual, erect, diminished. There is no case analysis to memorise.

misconceptions.belief: The image is diminished because the mirror is small.
misconceptions.correction: The image is diminished because the reflected rays diverge and their backward extensions meet close to the mirror, producing a smaller image. The size of the mirror glass is irrelevant; even a large convex mirror gives a diminished image.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State the three characteristics of the image formed by a convex mirror and where the image is located.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A convex mirror always forms an image that is virtual, erect, and diminished, no matter where the object is placed in front of the mirror. The image is always located behind the mirror, between the principal focus (F) and the pole (P). Because the reflected rays diverge after reflection, they never actually meet in front of the mirror; they only appear to meet when extended backwards behind the mirror. This is why the image is virtual (cannot be caught on a screen). The meeting point of the backward extensions lies closer to the mirror than the object, which makes the image smaller than the object, i.e., diminished. The backward extension preserves the upright orientation, so the image is erect. These three properties are fixed for every object position, which is the central result of this topic and the point CISCE examiners most often test.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why a convex mirror always forms a virtual image, even when the object is very far away.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A convex mirror has a reflecting surface that bulges outward, so it diverges any ray that strikes it -- the reflected rays spread apart. For a real image to form, reflected rays must actually converge and meet at a point in front of the mirror. Since the reflected rays from a convex mirror always diverge, they can never meet in front of the mirror, no matter how far or close the object is.
